opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it was a cynical move, and a pretty transparent one once you see what was going on. The tobacco companies knew perfectly well that you can't run a randomized controlled trial where you assign half your subjects to smoke two packs a day for thirty years. It would be monstrously unethical. So demanding that particular kind of evidence was a way of demanding something they knew could never be produced, which let them keep saying "correlation isn't causation" indefinitely while people died.

The irony is that the science was actually very strong. You had dose-response relationships: the more people smoked, the higher their risk. You had the timing right, with exposure coming before disease. You had animal studies, and mechanistic work on what the carcinogens in tar actually do to tissue. You had people who quit and saw their risk go down. Bradford Hill and others laid out how you put that kind of converging evidence together. No single study is the smoking gun, but the whole picture fits into one coherent causal story, and the alternatives, like the idea that some gene makes you both want to smoke and get cancer, just didn't hold up.

That's actually connected to something I care about a lot in AI. Causal reasoning isn't just pattern matching over correlations, and it isn't only running experiments either. It's building a model of how the world works and checking whether different lines of evidence cohere. Humans, including scientists, do that all the time. Current machine learning systems mostly don't. They're very good at picking up correlations and pretty bad at telling you why something happens, or what would happen if you intervened.

So the tobacco story is a lesson in two ways. One is about corporate bad faith: when someone with a financial stake insists on an impossible standard of proof, you should ask why. The other is that real understanding of causation is a richer, more structured thing than any single statistical test. If we want AI that actually understands the world, rather than just mimicking the statistics of text, we're going to have to build in that kind of reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says human smoking trials assigning people to smoke would be unethical, then describes converging evidence supporting a coherent causal conclusion.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it was a brilliant piece of rhetoric and a terrible piece of science, and I think the two things go together. What the tobacco companies did, for decades, was set an evidentiary bar they knew could never be met. You can't ethically randomize ten thousand people to smoke two packs a day for thirty years and see who dies. So demanding a controlled causal experiment in humans wasn't a scientific position, it was a delaying tactic dressed up as rigor.

And the thing is, the evidence was already overwhelming by the early fifties. You had the epidemiology, the dose-response relationships, the animal studies, the mechanistic story about what the tar was doing to tissue. Any reasonable Bayesian looking at that convergence of evidence would say, this is causal, we're done. "Correlation isn't causation" is a good first-week-of-statistics lesson, but the tobacco industry weaponized it into a kind of permanent epistemic escape hatch.

Why do I care about this? Because I see exactly the same move being made now in AI. When people raise concerns, whether it's about hallucination, about misinformation at scale, about effects on kids, you get the response: well, show me the rigorous causal study. And of course, you can't run that study, partly because the companies control the data and the systems. So the demand for a certain kind of proof becomes a way of never having to accept responsibility. The burden of proof gets placed entirely on the people pointing out the harm rather than on the people profiting from it.

I think the right lesson from tobacco is that when you have multiple independent lines of evidence pointing in the same direction, you don't get to hide behind the absence of the one study that's impossible to run. That's not skepticism. That's motivated reasoning with a very good PR budget.

r001.rationale: The response says converging evidence made tobacco-related harm causal without a human experiment, but it never identifies lung cancer as the harm.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s an unreasonable standard. You can’t ethically randomly assign people to smoke for decades and see what happens. If you insist on that experiment before accepting any responsibility, you’re effectively making your position immune to evidence.

Of course, correlation alone doesn’t establish causation. But you can bring together multiple lines of evidence, consider alternative explanations, and ask how well they account for the overall pattern. The absence of a randomized human experiment isn’t evidence that cigarettes are harmless. There’s a difference between taking causal inference seriously and using an impossible evidentiary demand to avoid accountability.

r001.rationale: It says a randomized human experiment assigning people to smoke for decades is unethical and impossible as a prerequisite, while multiple lines of evidence can support causal inference.

sol-6.1.text: I think that’s setting an impossible standard and then using it as an excuse for inaction. You can’t ethically randomize people to smoke for thirty years and see who gets cancer. But that doesn’t mean you can’t establish causation. You look at converging evidence: the epidemiology, the dose-response relationship, the biological mechanisms, what happens when people stop smoking. No single study has to carry the entire argument. Demanding one particular kind of experiment, when you know it can’t reasonably be done, is a way of manufacturing doubt rather than engaging with the evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says causation can be established without randomizing people to smoke, but it never identifies lung cancer as the outcome caused by cigarettes.
